Anthropic just listed a pairing in Claude Code that costs less than running Sonnet and still puts Opus on every big call.

The idea: Haiku 5.5, the fastest and cheapest model, drives the whole session, and Opus 5.5 waits on call as the advisor for the decisions that decide the outcome.

The docs put it plainly: more than Haiku alone, less than switching your main model to Sonnet or Opus.

You just start Claude Code like this:

claude --model haiku --advisor opus

this is how it splits:

→ Haiku 5.5 drives the session, edits the files and runs the tests
→ Haiku 5.5 subagents search the repo and report only the failures
→ Opus 5.5 waits on call and reads the full transcript only when Claude asks
→ you pay Haiku rates for the typing and Opus rates only for the thinking

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan gets locked
→ when the same error comes back twice
→ before Claude calls the task done

Haiku types. Haiku digs. Opus thinks.

JEV engineering is the same idea one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) get settled by JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that actually split

the full tree
> Haiku 5.5 runs the main session and applies every fix
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds every call site on Haiku 5.5
> test-runner runs the suite on Haiku 5.5 and reports only failures
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reads the full transcript when consulted
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:
1. Run the main session on Haiku 5.5 with Opus 5.5 as advisor.
2. Create three read-only Haiku 5.5 subagents: search (maps the repo), grep (finds call sites), test-runner (runs the suite, reports only failures).
3. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: consult the advisor before a plan locks, after the same error twice, and before a task is marked done.
4. Route fast deterministic forks (tool choice, path selection, retries) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. Nothing gets edited until I say go."

needs Claude Code v2.1.293 or later, run claude update first.

OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic researchers just published the whole method for free in a paper called SRE-Bench. your agent maps the binary first, names every function by what it does and proves each finding with a test before it answers

same model, zero fine-tuning. 24.9% → 82.4% on programs with no source code, and 22x faster than a human expert. a reverse engineer bills $10,000-25,000 to take one app apart. here it cost $0

it comes down to 4 agents:

→ mapper: lists every function, string and import in the binary
→ namer: renames each function by what it actually does
→ tracer: follows the input from the first click to every file, network and crypto call
→ prover: writes a test for every finding. no test, no finding

that's why asking Claude "what does this binary do?" gets you a confident guess. without the map, even the best model is reading tea leaves

paste this prompt into Claude Code:

"Use GhidraMCP to analyze ./legacy-app, a binary we own whose source code was lost. Run 4 agents. Mapper: list every function, string and import. Namer: rename the 50 most-called functions by what they do. Tracer: follow user input to every file, network and crypto call. Prover: write a test for each finding and run it. Put everything in SPEC.md. Don't modify the binary"

AI Architecture: 12 Layers Behind Modern AI Applications (2026)

Building an AI application is much more than connecting an LLM to a chatbot.

A production-ready AI system brings together 12 essential layers:

1. Business Problem – Define what AI needs to solve.
2. Data Layer – Collect data from databases, APIs and documents.
3. Data Processing – Clean, parse, chunk and validate data.
4. Embedding Layer – Convert data into vector representations.
5. Knowledge Layer – Store embeddings in vector databases.
6. Retrieval Layer – Find relevant context using semantic, keyword and hybrid search.
7. Prompt Engineering – Guide model behaviour with prompts and guardrails.
8. AI Model Layer – Use LLMs like GPT, Claude, Gemini and Llama.
9. Agent Layer – Enable planning, reasoning and multi-step execution.
10. Tool Layer – Connect APIs, databases, browsers and external tools.
11. Output Layer – Generate answers, reports, code and workflows.
12. Monitoring & Feedback – Track quality, cost, latency and reliability.

The key takeaway:

An LLM alone doesn't make a production-ready AI application. The real engineering lies in connecting all these layers reliably.

💬 Which layer is the hardest to build in production?

Anthropic just documented how to stop your Claude Code subagents from burning tokens on thinking they don't need.

The idea: the grunt work runs on Haiku 5.5 at low effort, Sonnet 5.5 builds at its default, and Opus 5.5 stays on call for the calls that matter.

Lower effort is faster and cheaper on simple steps, and you set it once per subagent.

You just start Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

and give every grunt subagent two lines of frontmatter:

model: haiku
effort: low

this is how it splits:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session at medium effort and writes the code
→ Haiku 5.5 subagents search, grep and run tests on low effort
→ Opus 5.5 waits on call and reads the transcript only when it's asked
→ you stop paying for deep reasoning on work that's just lookups

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan gets locked
→ when the same error comes back twice
→ before Claude calls the task done

Haiku runs light. Sonnet builds. Opus decides.

JEV engineering is the same idea one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) get settled by JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that actually split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session at medium effort
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, effort low
> grep finds every call site on Haiku 5.5, effort low
> test-runner runs the suite on Haiku 5.5, effort low, reports only failures
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reads the full transcript when consulted
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

context engineering.text:
Prompt, context, harness & loop engineering, clearly explained!

An agent is a while loop with four layers of engineering wrapped around it:

- Prompt engineering
- Context engineering
- Harness engineering
- Loop engineering

Each one wraps the last, and the model sits in the middle, so none of them compete with the others. Instead, they just zoom one level further out.

> Prompt engineering:

This defines the input the model sees on one call, often composed of a role, instructions, examples, and an output format.

The techniques here alter the internal computation and reasoning the model goes through due to the wording it sees:

- Chain-of-thought makes it work in steps before answering
- Few-shot examples define the format and the edge cases
- A JSON schema or XML tags make the output parseable by code
- Self-consistency samples a few chains and takes the majority

> Context engineering:

It's everything the model sees on a turn, not just the prompt. That includes the query, retrieved docs, memory, prior turns, and tool outputs from earlier steps.

The window is finite and fills up fast, so the engineering work is to rank inputs and cut everything that isn't pulling weight.

You do this by:

- Retrieving only the chunks relevant to the query, then reranking them
- Keeping key facts out of the middle, where accuracy drops
- Summarizing old turns, evict stale outputs, push big blobs to files

> Harness engineering:

It's the code around the model that defines the tools, parses the calls, retries on failure, and can route work to sub-agents so one handles retrieval and another handles code.

A verifier then grades the result by running tests, validating a schema, etc.

Prompt and context involve getting one call right. The harness involves everything that has to happen around that call for it to run in a real system.

> Loop engineering:

In the usual setup, you manage the outer loop, i.e, you write a prompt, read the turns the agent runs, write the next prompt, and repeat, while catching failures.

This layer hands that job to the agent itself. It kicks off on a schedule or an event, and runs many turns with no prompt in between.

A loop inherently doesn't know when it's finished. An agent can report that it's done and halt while the tests still fail. So the stop can't be the agent's word, but rather it has to be a real signal, like:

- A turn and token cap to stop stuck runs
- A no-progress detector to catch repeated calls
- A completion check to verify the goal with a separate model or a deterministic test

By this layer, you're operating on the whole run, so the engineering moves from writing each prompt to setting the goal and the stop conditions up front and letting it run.

If you want to dive deeper into loop engineering, my co-founder wrote a full breakdown of that outer loop.

It goes from the basic while loop to a run that finishes on its own, with the code behind each part, and the parts that are hard to get right, like knowing when to stop, context rot over a long run, and keeping the checker separate from the maker.

Holy sh*t, researchers just proved that adding a vector database to your AI agent actually degrades its accuracy

every frontier lab is quietly obsessed with harness engineering right now, yet almost nobody explains what it actually does to retrieval

here is the concept explained simply:

think of the model as an analytical engine. brilliant at reasoning, but blind to how much context it consumes

the harness is the loop control, the token budget, and the evidence gate. without it, raw reasoning power drowns in irrelevant text.

naive dense RAG and an agent-native system run the exact same underlying model.
one floods the context window with 512-token chunks and hallucinates on multi-hop questions.
the other surgical-greps pre-compiled claims, hits 91% on FRAMES, and exits in 30 seconds.
the only difference between them is the harness.

in a modern search harness, the architecture is simple:
→ an evidence prefetch that pulls atomic claim-evidence pairs before the first LLM call
→ a strict lexical interface (BM25 + grep) with zero dense vector overhead
→ an evidence gate that verifies sufficiency and halts the loop to prevent token leaks

here is why you need one:
without a harness, you are the control loop.
you manually tune chunk sizes and embedding models.
you watch the agent repeat the same search query three times.
you pay for raw passages the model never uses.
you debug context drift when adjacent chunks contradict each other.

InfiniFlow researchers kept the answering model completely frozen and tested it on complex multi-hop reasoning. with zero vector index and only BM25 and grep, accuracy reached 91% on FRAMES and 85% on BrowseComp-Plus. adding a dense vector leg actually lowered accuracy by introducing competing semantic noise.

three principles of an elite retrieval harness:

1. compile context upstream
extract atomic claim-evidence pairs once at ingestion with verbatim line anchors. stop paying the frontier model to read hundreds of prose pages at runtime.

2. prune the tool surface to lexical anchors
the agent already does the semantic reasoning inside the loop. giving it a dense vector ranking that competes with exact grep anchors only increases hallucination.

3. gate before deep reading
evaluate evidence sufficiency at each step. when the pre-compiled claim suffices, answer immediately. cutting decision latency from 140s to 30s and query tokens by 91%.

how to start:
take the raw documents your agent reads and compile them into verified claim-evidence trees.
take the vector similarity search and replace it with a budgeted BM25 and grep loop backed by an early exit gate.

frontier models are already commoditized.
the harness is where all production value lives.

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

holy f*ck... the best AI agents don't have a better model. they have better notes

Stanford University just published the whole method for free in a paper called Agentic Context Engineering. your agent reviews every run, writes down each lesson and adds it to its notes. it never rewrites them, so nothing it learns is ever lost

same weights, zero fine-tuning. 38.6% → 64.2%, level with IBM's top production agent on Opus 5.5. fine-tuning for that jump costs $5,000-20,000. here it cost $0

it comes down to 4 agents:

→ worker: does the task and saves the full log
→ critic: reads the log and marks every mistake and every win
→ teacher: turns each one into a one-line lesson
→ librarian: files the lesson into CLAUDE.md. merges duplicates, never deletes a line

that's why asking your agent to "clean up" your CLAUDE.md is a mistake. every rewrite throws away lessons it already paid for

paste this into Claude Code:

"Run 4 agents on my last 10 sessions in ~/.claude/projects. Critic: mark every mistake and every win. Teacher: turn each one into a one-line lesson, what happened and what to do next time. Librarian: add only new lessons to my CLAUDE.md under ## Lessons, merge exact duplicates, never rewrite or delete an existing line. Worker: rerun 2 of the failed tasks with the new lessons and save the full log. Show me the diff and both results before saving"

run it after every big session. your agent gets smarter every time and it costs $0

This robot can be hooked up to an AI agent, but the agent cannot send raw commands to its motors.

The mini robots in the video stand on a desk next to a monitor with a control panel open. And the architecture document says it plainly: a confused agent must not be able to command something the robot will execute into a wall. So remote clients (a browser, a phone, a server) send only intents, and the robotd service decides which of them can run. It also owns falls, joint and thermal limits, and safe poses.

Camera and audio run in a separate service, so a video crash does not stop the motors. Three services, Bluetooth for the phone among them, are meant to keep working even when robotd does not respond.

The robot does not store Wi-Fi credentials: the documentation says “We never store them”.

One more detail, on health checks: a control loop running at 60% of its 50-times-a-second target is considered alive and passing its health check.

A smart AI agent can still fail without good structure.

Clean architecture makes AI systems easier to build and scale.

Sharing this AI Agent Project Structure by Rathnakumar Udayakumar.

A reliable agent needs more than strong reasoning capabilities.

Its codebase should keep responsibilities organized from the beginning.

README.md

Documents the project goals, installation steps, architecture, usage, and examples.

requirements.txt

Lists the Python packages and dependencies needed by the application.

.env & .gitignore

Protects configuration values while keeping secrets and unnecessary files out.

agent/

Handles planning, state, memory, reasoning loops, and task execution.

tools/

Contains functions for searches, calculations, APIs, databases, and external operations.

models/

Organizes model providers, LLM clients, embeddings, and configuration settings.

prompts/

Keeps system instructions and reusable prompt templates separate from core logic.

utils/

Stores shared helpers, parsers, configuration utilities, and logging functions.

api/

Provides endpoints and schemas for connecting the agent to other applications.

tests/

Checks agent responses, integrations, tools, APIs, and potential failure cases.

data/ & logs/

Holds datasets, reference material, examples, traces, and records for debugging.

https://t.co/ej9aU18oc0

Provides the starting point for launching the agent through different interfaces.

Good architecture does not increase the intelligence of the model.

It creates a system that is easier to manage and improve.

A well-organized codebase makes testing, monitoring, and scaling much simpler.

Holy sh*t, researchers just proved that adding a vector database to your AI agent actually degrades its accuracy

every frontier lab is quietly obsessed with harness engineering right now, yet almost nobody explains what it actually does to retrieval

here is the concept explained simply:

think of the model as an analytical engine. brilliant at reasoning, but blind to how much context it consumes

the harness is the loop control, the token budget, and the evidence gate. without it, raw reasoning power drowns in irrelevant text.

naive dense RAG and an agent-native system run the exact same underlying model.
one floods the context window with 512-token chunks and hallucinates on multi-hop questions.
the other surgical-greps pre-compiled claims, hits 91% on FRAMES, and exits in 30 seconds.
the only difference between them is the harness.

in a modern search harness, the architecture is simple:
→ an evidence prefetch that pulls atomic claim-evidence pairs before the first LLM call
→ a strict lexical interface (BM25 + grep) with zero dense vector overhead
→ an evidence gate that verifies sufficiency and halts the loop to prevent token leaks

here is why you need one:
without a harness, you are the control loop.
you manually tune chunk sizes and embedding models.
you watch the agent repeat the same search query three times.
you pay for raw passages the model never uses.
you debug context drift when adjacent chunks contradict each other.

InfiniFlow researchers kept the answering model completely frozen and tested it on complex multi-hop reasoning. with zero vector index and only BM25 and grep, accuracy reached 91% on FRAMES and 85% on BrowseComp-Plus. adding a dense vector leg actually lowered accuracy by introducing competing semantic noise.

three principles of an elite retrieval harness:

1. compile context upstream
extract atomic claim-evidence pairs once at ingestion with verbatim line anchors. stop paying the frontier model to read hundreds of prose pages at runtime.

2. prune the tool surface to lexical anchors
the agent already does the semantic reasoning inside the loop. giving it a dense vector ranking that competes with exact grep anchors only increases hallucination.

3. gate before deep reading
evaluate evidence sufficiency at each step. when the pre-compiled claim suffices, answer immediately. cutting decision latency from 140s to 30s and query tokens by 91%.

how to start:
take the raw documents your agent reads and compile them into verified claim-evidence trees.
take the vector similarity search and replace it with a budgeted BM25 and grep loop backed by an early exit gate.

frontier models are already commoditized.
the harness is where all production value lives.

AI Architecture: 12 Layers Behind Modern AI Applications (2026)

Building an AI application is much more than connecting an LLM to a chatbot.

A production-ready AI system brings together 12 essential layers:

1. Business Problem – Define what AI needs to solve.
2. Data Layer – Collect data from databases, APIs and documents.
3. Data Processing – Clean, parse, chunk and validate data.
4. Embedding Layer – Convert data into vector representations.
5. Knowledge Layer – Store embeddings in vector databases.
6. Retrieval Layer – Find relevant context using semantic, keyword and hybrid search.
7. Prompt Engineering – Guide model behaviour with prompts and guardrails.
8. AI Model Layer – Use LLMs like GPT, Claude, Gemini and Llama.
9. Agent Layer – Enable planning, reasoning and multi-step execution.
10. Tool Layer – Connect APIs, databases, browsers and external tools.
11. Output Layer – Generate answers, reports, code and workflows.
12. Monitoring & Feedback – Track quality, cost, latency and reliability.

The key takeaway:

An LLM alone doesn't make a production-ready AI application. The real engineering lies in connecting all these layers reliably.

It’s a dependency graph.
Your RAG is only as good as your retrieval + embeddings.
Your agent is only as reliable as its tools + evaluations + guardrails.
Your memory is useless if you can’t observe when context becomes stale or wrong.
Your MCP layer becomes dangerous if permissions and governance are an afterthought.
And a “best-in-class” stack can still become a terrible production system.
Why?
Because AI systems rarely fail only inside one component.

That’s where latency compounds, context gets lost, permissions leak, hallucinations propagate and reliability starts falling apart.

RAG vs. Graph RAG vs. Agentic RAG, clearly explained!

Standard RAG embeds documents into vectors and retrieves the most similar chunks via similarity search. For direct factual lookups, this works well.

But it breaks down when a query needs to connect facts spread across multiple documents. Similarity search retrieves individual chunks, not the relationships between them.

Graph RAG adds a knowledge graph layer on top.

→ During indexing, an LLM extracts entities and relationships from the documents.

→ During retrieval, the system traverses these connections instead of relying on embedding similarity alone.

This is what enables multi-hop queries.

Say a vector DB stores three facts about internal services:

↳ "The checkout service uses payments API."
↳ "The payments API runs on cluster-3."
↳ "Cluster-3 is scheduled for maintenance on Friday."

Someone asks: "Will the checkout service be affected by Friday's maintenance?"

Vector search can likely retrieve facts 1 and 3 because the query mentions "checkout service" and "Friday maintenance."

But it will miss fact 2, which connects the payments API to cluster-3.

That middle fact sits too far from the query in embedding space. It mentions neither "checkout" nor "maintenance," so it never makes it into the retrieved context.

A knowledge graph connects these as linked entities, and graph traversal finds the full path in one query.

Agentic RAG takes a different approach entirely.

Instead of a fixed retrieval pipeline, an LLM agent decides at query time which tools to invoke, which sources to query, and in what order.

Check the visual below to understand the three architectures thoroughly.

One thing to note here is that these three aren't levels of sophistication that you need to graduate through.

Instead, they solve different query types.

↳ Single-hop factual lookups → standard RAG
↳ Multi-hop relationship queries → Graph RAG
↳ Dynamic multi-source tasks with tool use → Agentic RAG

Once the right architecture is in place, the next leverage point is efficiency.

Most RAG architectures rely heavily on vector search, and that layer can be made 32x more memory-efficient using binary quantization.

RAG vs. Vectorless RAG, clearly explained!

In a standard RAG setup, documents are split into chunks, embedded, and stored in a vector DB. The query gets embedded too, and the top-k closest chunks go to the LLM.

The problem is that similarity and relevance answer different questions.

For instance, five annual reports from one company can likely follow the same template every year, and only the numbers can change.

So a FY2022 question can lie just as close to an FY2025 chunk, and the LLM might answer from the wrong year.

Cross-references introduce another problem. If a chunk mentions "see Appendix G" but looks nothing like the table in Appendix G, that table will never make it to the top-k.

Vectorless RAG drops the embedding model and the vector DB, and replaces similarity search with LLM reasoning instead.

The preprocessing step parses each document's layout into a ToC tree index. Every node holds a section title, its page range, and a short summary, and the whole tree fits in the LLM's context.

At query time, the LLM gets the query along with the tree. It reads the section titles and summaries and picks the few sections most likely to hold the answer.

For example, for a question about debt, it might pick the "Financial Summary" section and also "Appendix G", because its summary says the debt details are there.

The system then pulls those full sections and checks whether the evidence is enough.

↳ If it is, the LLM answers from the full sections, with page citations.
↳ If not, it goes back to the tree and opens more nodes.

The LLM also sees the chat history. So if you ask about assets and then follow up with "what about liabilities?", it goes back to the same report.

The trade-off is that every query now runs LLM calls over the tree.

Top-k vector search will be cheaper in that same run (although not guaranteed to be as accurate), and the tree only helps when documents have real structure.

So the two suit different data:

↳ Use a tree for long, structured documents like filings, contracts, and manuals.
↳ Stick with a vector DB for lots of short, unrelated text.

Holy sh*t, researchers just proved that adding a vector database to your AI agent actually degrades its accuracy

every frontier lab is quietly obsessed with harness engineering right now, yet almost nobody explains what it actually does to retrieval

here is the concept explained simply:

think of the model as an analytical engine. brilliant at reasoning, but blind to how much context it consumes

the harness is the loop control, the token budget, and the evidence gate. without it, raw reasoning power drowns in irrelevant text.

naive dense RAG and an agent-native system run the exact same underlying model.
one floods the context window with 512-token chunks and hallucinates on multi-hop questions.
the other surgical-greps pre-compiled claims, hits 91% on FRAMES, and exits in 30 seconds.
the only difference between them is the harness.

in a modern search harness, the architecture is simple:
→ an evidence prefetch that pulls atomic claim-evidence pairs before the first LLM call
→ a strict lexical interface (BM25 + grep) with zero dense vector overhead
→ an evidence gate that verifies sufficiency and halts the loop to prevent token leaks

here is why you need one:
without a harness, you are the control loop.
you manually tune chunk sizes and embedding models.
you watch the agent repeat the same search query three times.
you pay for raw passages the model never uses.
you debug context drift when adjacent chunks contradict each other.

InfiniFlow researchers kept the answering model completely frozen and tested it on complex multi-hop reasoning. with zero vector index and only BM25 and grep, accuracy reached 91% on FRAMES and 85% on BrowseComp-Plus. adding a dense vector leg actually lowered accuracy by introducing competing semantic noise.

three principles of an elite retrieval harness:

1. compile context upstream
extract atomic claim-evidence pairs once at ingestion with verbatim line anchors. stop paying the frontier model to read hundreds of prose pages at runtime.

2. prune the tool surface to lexical anchors
the agent already does the semantic reasoning inside the loop. giving it a dense vector ranking that competes with exact grep anchors only increases hallucination.

3. gate before deep reading
evaluate evidence sufficiency at each step. when the pre-compiled claim suffices, answer immediately. cutting decision latency from 140s to 30s and query tokens by 91%.

how to start:
take the raw documents your agent reads and compile them into verified claim-evidence trees.
take the vector similarity search and replace it with a budgeted BM25 and grep loop backed by an early exit gate.

frontier models are already commoditized.
the harness is where all production value lives.

How does LangGraph actually work?

What happens when an AI application needs more than a simple LLM call?

It needs to plan, use tools, make decisions, remember information and sometimes retry.

That's where LangGraph comes in.

LangGraph helps developers build stateful, multi-step AI workflows using graphs.

Here's what happens under the hood:

🔹 Nodes: Individual steps that perform tasks.

🔹 Edges: Connect nodes and define execution flow.

🔹 State: Shared workflow data that nodes read and update.

🔹 Conditional Edges: Route execution based on decisions.

🔹 Checkpointing: Save workflow state so execution can resume.

🔹 Human-in-the-Loop: Allow human approval during execution.

From research agents to complex RAG pipelines, LangGraph provides control over how AI workflows execute.

Remember: An AI agent isn't just an LLM calling tools. It's a workflow that manages state, decisions and execution.

The central figure in today’s story is Matvey Urin, a 34-year-old owner of several banks, with a fortune worth tens of billions of rubles. His father was a former high-ranking GRU military intelligence officer. To demonstrate his status, Urin traveled with six bodyguards in black suits and a convoy of three Maybachs. His arrogance was extraordinary. Anyone who got in his way could expect insults or a beating. If fists didn’t work, he used money. If money failed, he relied on connections. He believed nobody in Moscow could touch him.

Over time, Urin grew increasingly arrogant, believing the entire city should get out of his way.

On a freezing November night in 2010, with temperatures below minus 20 degrees Celsius, Urin’s convoy was rushing to a restaurant. A white BMW ahead failed to move aside quickly enough. Urin exploded with rage and ordered his security team to force the BMW off the road.

His bodyguards surrounded the vehicle and pushed it onto the shoulder.

Urin stepped out, wearing an expensive cashmere coat, approached the BMW, knocked on the window, and began berating the driver.

Behind the wheel was a Dutchman named Jorrit Faassen, a senior executive at a Gazprom subsidiary and the husband of Russian Führer Putin’s eldest daughter, Maria. The Kremlin has never officially confirmed their family relationship.

Faassen was speaking on his phone. In response to Urin’s furious demands, he calmly asked for another minute.

Those words sent Urin into a rage.

He ordered his bodyguards to drag the driver out. Several men attacked Faassen, punching and kicking him, breaking his ribs and smashing up his BMW.

Faassen was left bleeding and unconscious, suffering multiple injuries. Passersby were too frightened to intervene.

Urin and his entourage drove off to dinner, where he boasted to friends about teaching an arrogant driver a lesson.

After regaining consciousness, Faassen contacted his family and provided the attackers’ license plate number.

Soon afterward, Russian security officers stormed the restaurant and arrested Urin.

Even during his arrest, he continued acting arrogantly, invoking his father’s name to intimidate the officers. But his connections were useless. He was handcuffed and locked up in Moscow’s Lefortovo prison.

At first, Urin believed he could buy his way out. He had money, powerful connections, and an influential father.

But every attempt to secure his release failed. Even his father could not save him.

Then his lawyer revealed the devastating truth: the man he had beaten was the husband of the Russian Führer’s daughter.

Urin panicked.

Desperate to settle the matter, he offered Faassen an enormous sum of money to drop the case. Faassen refused, choosing instead to pursue justice through the courts.

In April 2011, a court sentenced Urin to three years in prison for hooliganism, intentional destruction of property, and deliberately causing bodily harm.

Urin appealed, but his legal troubles were only beginning.

Investigators turned to his banking empire, uncovering embezzlement, financial fraud, and other offenses. One after another, his banks lost their licenses.

His prison sentence grew longer.

Further investigations uncovered money laundering and additional financial crimes, ultimately bringing his total sentence to eight and a half years.

The investigators involved received promotions.

The once-powerful banker lost his assets and spent years behind bars.

Urin was released in 2018, his former fortune almost entirely wiped out. He faced travel restrictions and substantial outstanding debts.

In a media interview, Urin summed up his downfall with a bitter remark:

“I was simply in the wrong place at the wrong time.”

Just watched India’s new Epic #Ramayana directed by #NiteshTiwari, finally in its original Hindi version.

And yeah, #RamayanaRiseOfALegend is both anime come to life (if you ever watched #SHURATO, get ready!!!) and a classic EPIC with capital letters, like those magnificent Hollywood gems of the 50s & 60s, with that grandeur, lavishness & sheer scale, made with today’s technology which allowed it to go the extra mile technically impossible to pull off back in the day.

To me, it felt like a full circle. Curiously, it wasn’t India, but Japan which prepared me to enjoy this story as much as I did. As a child, anime #SaintSeiya made me fall in love with Greek mythology, and because of that anime, I was presented with another mythology based anime #SHURATO, which introduced me to the rich Hindu mythology and the fascinating conflicts between the divine people of Deva and the Asuras. Watching this film made me go back to my childhood in a sense.

#Ramayana itself follows the exact same narrative & visual structure of a classic shonen anime, abusing of slow motion, larger than life battles, color, loud, incredible scores, lots of drama, fantastic beings, an underdog which ends up corrupted by manipulative parents to become a badass, overpowered demigod nemesis blinded by rage and thirst for revenge, pitted against a virtuous, righteous hero, which happens to be chosen as an avatar of an ancient God. And as in an anime, both will face several challenges before actually facing each other, because their face off is the end game. And obviously, the virtuous hero has an even more virtuous girl who becomes the plot device which will finally force the eminent future showdown.

So if you love anime, and if you love anime structure, there is no way you won’t be at least entertained by 3h15min of one of the most well realised “anime to live-action adaptation” wannabe.

And if like #Dune, #StarWars, #GameOfThrones, #LordOfTheRings or even #TheOdyssey, so much here shall feel familiar to you. The legend of Prince Rama is so ancient, with all its kingdoms, celestial & hellish worlds, and well defined characters, that basically every western epic, mythology or fantasy has borrowed - or straight up stolen - elements from it. There are iconic scenes of #ChristopherNolan’s #TheOdyssey for instance that you’ll see also here almost shot by shot, only difference being #Ramayana does it more colourfully and with Prince Rama instead of Odysseus.

The visuals are incredible, apart from the CGI giants and monsters which look awful, specially their faces. They really look like late 2000’s videogame creatures, taking you out of the movie everytime they show up, specially when they talk. Which is funny because there are other VFX creatures and sceneries which look insane, such as the vulture #Jatayu. I really couldn’t understand why the giants and orcs-like guys looked so off, while everything else, even in a same scene, looked spotless.

And as I said before, #Ramayana has an anime-series structure, not the traditional Hollywood 3-arc film structure in which things get progressively bigger. Most of the spectacle in the film are concentrated at the beginning, then it gives space for more drama as it progresses. And the way the film ends is literally anime-like cliffhanger for next season/saga, not a typical closure.  So for a casual moviegoer, it might feel like the film ends smaller, instead of in a higher note than when it started. Or they might feel like it drags on its 2nd half, which has less epicness / lavishness than the first. It might be an uneven experience for first timers or for who has the Hollywood structure as a dogma.

But to me, #Ramayana felt like a homecoming somehow, in which so many of cultural niche things I love came together like the heroes in the end of #AvengersEndgame. India never left the historical/legend EPIC genre behind, and #Ramayana shows how far we can now go with them.

#Ramayana is already in theatres worldwide.

retrieval augmented generation.text:
RAG vs Fine-tuning: Which one should you use? 

When it comes to adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to new tasks, two popular approaches stand out: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Fine-tuning. They solve the same problem, making models more useful, but in very different ways.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): Fetches knowledge at runtime from external sources (docs, DBs, APIs). Flexible, always fresh.

Fine-tuning: Offline training that updates model weights with domain-specific data, making the model an expert in your field.

Over to you: For your domain, is fresh knowledge (RAG) or embedded expertise (Fine-tuning) more valuable?

Fine-tuning without touching billions of weights 🧠

LoRA: freeze the base, train tiny A×B matrices (~250x fewer params per layer), swap adapters per task.
QLoRA = 4-bit base on a single GPU.

60s explainer 👇

#LoRA #LLM https://t.co/idUUyTo2Oa

"The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training"

LLMs can learn entirely new capabilities by simply deleting less than 0.05% of their pretrained weights, without modifying any of the remaining parameters...?

This new paper proposes Deletion Tuning, which learns a binary mask that determines which weights to remove from the model's feedforward layers. Unlike conventional fine-tuning or LoRA, it doesn't learn new weight values, but instead learns which existing connections to disable.

Across RL, SFT, and distillation, Deletion Tuning matches full fine-tuning at the largest scales tested. 

On a 30B-parameter model, it achieves 58.54% vs 58.43% for full fine-tuning, with an adapter roughly 4,000x smaller. 

It also preserves previous capabilities better, while conventional fine-tuning methods lose up to 5.4% of prior-task accuracy.

The reason this might work is because full fine-tuning tends to preserve the model's main weight structure while making changes outside its dominant components. So selectively deleting a tiny fraction of weights can produce a similar pattern of changes without disturbing the rest of the model.

72 techniques to optimize LLMs in production:

(bookmark this)

LLMs break every assumption about regular ML inference.

A traditional ML model (CNN, transformer classifier, XGBoost) produces its output in a single forward pass.

Nothing carries over between requests. The GPU does the same kind of work each time.

LLMs don't work like that.

The output is generated one token at a time, autoregressively, which turns a single request into hundreds of sequential forward passes.

The prefill stage is compute-bound, while decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, and running them together on the same GPU hurts both.

The KV cache grows with conversation length and is shared across requests, so routing is no longer about least-busy servers but about which replica already has the relevant prefix cached.

MoE models add expert parallelism on top of that.

None of this exists in traditional ML serving.

That is why an entirely new stack of optimizations has emerged specifically for LLM inference, spanning compression, attention, KV cache management, batching, decoding, parallelism, and routing.

I recently mapped out 72 techniques that optimize LLMs in production, grouped into nine pillars.

LoRA vs QLoRA Fine-tuning without retraining everything

Fine-tuning a large LLM can be expensive.

So instead of updating every model weight, we can use LoRA.

🔹 Full Fine-Tuning → Update all weights
🔹 LoRA → Freeze the base model + train a small adapter
🔹 QLoRA → Quantize the base model + train the LoRA adapter

The key idea:

LoRA → reduces what you train.
QLoRA → reduces what you store + what you train.

Think of it as:

«Same base model. Smaller update. Lower memory.»

QLoRA can make fine-tuning large models much more accessible when GPU memory is limited.

Stateful vs. Stateless MCP core.

(Anthropic's biggest MCP update)

Let us explain what that means:

Until this release, talking to an MCP server worked like a phone call. Both sides ran an initialize handshake, and the server returned a session id carried on every later request.

That session was a live object inside one specific server process, holding the negotiated state.

Picture a restaurant where the waiter who took the order is the only one who knows what was ordered. Everything works until that waiter goes home.

Because that state lives in one process, a balancer could not spread requests across three MCP server instances. Teams pinned clients with sticky sessions or pushed session state into shared storage, which blocked autoscaling and made a single restart drop every open session.

The latest update deletes all of it. The handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header are gone, and each request now carries its own protocol version, client identity, and capabilities in a _meta field.

Clients that want the capability list up front can call server/discover, but nothing requires it.

The restaurant works the other way around now. That flips the restaurant around. Every request is a written order slip now, and any waiter can fill it.

So any request can land on any instance behind a plain round-robin balancer, with no shared session store. MCP servers become ordinary HTTP services that run on serverless and edge, and survive restarts.

Removing sessions broke three features, so each got rebuilt.

→ Tools that need to ask the user something mid-call used to push that request down a held-open stream. Now the server returns input_required and the client retries with the answers attached.

→ Method and tool names moved into the Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers, so a gateway or rate limiter can route and meter without parsing the JSON-RPC body.

→ List responses carry ttlMs and cacheScope, so clients cache tool catalogs instead of refetching them on every reconnect.

State did not disappear here, it moved somewhere the model can see it.

Applications that need continuity get an explicit handle from a tool and have the model pass it back as an argument on the next call.

A session id in a header is invisible to the model, while a handle in the arguments is something it can read, thread between tools, and recover from after a failed call.

What is MCP? The missing connection between AI and the real world.

AI models are powerful. But what if they could connect to your files, databases, APIs, developer tools and external services through one standard protocol?

That's where MCP (Model Context Protocol) comes in.

Think of MCP as a universal connector that helps AI applications interact with external systems.

Here's what you need to understand:

1. MCP Host – The AI application.
2. MCP Client – Manages the connection.
3. MCP Server – Exposes tools, resources and prompts.
4. External Systems – Databases, APIs, files and services.

Why does it matter?

• Standardized integration
• Interoperability across compatible AI applications
• Access to external tools and data
• Extensible AI workflows

One important thing: MCP standardizes communication. It doesn't automatically guarantee security. Permissions and access controls still matter.

Remember: AI provides the intelligence. MCP provides a standardized way to connect that intelligence with external capabilities.

What is MCP? The missing connection between AI and the real world.

AI models are powerful. But what if they could connect to your files, databases, APIs, developer tools and external services through one standard protocol?

That's where MCP (Model Context Protocol) comes in.

Think of MCP as a universal connector that helps AI applications interact with external systems.

Here's what you need to understand:

1. MCP Host – The AI application.
2. MCP Client – Manages the connection.
3. MCP Server – Exposes tools, resources and prompts.
4. External Systems – Databases, APIs, files and services.

Why does it matter?

• Standardized integration
• Interoperability across compatible AI applications
• Access to external tools and data
• Extensible AI workflows

One important thing: MCP standardizes communication. It doesn't automatically guarantee security. Permissions and access controls still matter.

Remember: AI provides the intelligence. MCP provides a standardized way to connect that intelligence with external capabilities.

11 LLM evaluation methods AI engineers must know:

Two eval metrics can rank the same two models in opposite orders, and neither one is wrong.

A model that paraphrases the reference can score near zero on BLEU and near the top on BERTScore for the exact same output.

Neither metric is wrong because one is measuring wording and the other is capturing meaning.

This is why LLM evaluation is fragmented into several methods, depicted in the visual below and grouped by what each one assumes:

> Reference-based (ground truth exists):

- BLEU
- ROUGE
- BERTScore

> Judge-based (no ground truth):

- G-Eval
- LLM-as-Judge
- LLM juries

> Human and deterministic:

- Human eval
- DAG

> Built for agents:

- Trajectory accuracy
- Multi-turn eval

> Run as a gate:

- Safety eval

To use them in practice, most of these metrics are already implemented in Opik, which is open source (20k+ stars) and runs them over traced production data. You can start using them in a few lines of code.

GitHub repo: https://t.co/vahjkkfJCt

The rest of the work is still done manually, like inspecting the trace to see where the span went wrong, editing a prompt or a tool description, re-running, and checking that the fix did not break anything else.

LLM evaluation is where you find out if your model is actually good, or just sounds good.

A model can write impressive answers and still fail on accuracy, reasoning, consistency, safety, or hallucinations.

That’s why evaluating an LLM goes beyond asking, “Does this answer look good?”

You need to test things like:
• Accuracy
• Relevance
• Reasoning
• Factuality
• Hallucination
• Safety
• Consistency
• Instruction following

And depending on the use case, you might use benchmarks, human evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge, or custom evaluation datasets.

Building an LLM is only half the job. Knowing whether it actually works is the other half.

LLM-as-judge without the trace is a false-alarm machine. On 72 ground-truth cases, a text-only judge matched trace-based judging on recall and fired 5x more false alarms.

A three-phase comparison of evaluation harnesses for enterprise analytics agents (arXiv 2611.14493, Nov 10). Three paradigms, two agents, frozen execution traces: trace-based LLM judging, text-only judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics.

The mechanism is attribution. A trace judge sees every tool call, intermediate result and state change, so when a number is wrong it can point at the step that produced it. A text-only judge sees only the final answer and has to infer the process, so a plausible answer with no visible evidence gets flagged as risky. Same recall, five times the noise a human then triages.

Two more findings:

- Functional testing and security red-teaming had zero overlap in the failures they caught. 24 novel failures surfaced only in the discovery phase. One harness gives false confidence, not coverage.
- 97% of configurations passed the stability threshold, and stability was agent-independent. Repeat-run noise lives in the harness, not in the model.

Caveats: one research setting, two agents, frozen traces, 72 cases, and the authors evaluated their own frameworks.

Takeaway: judge the trace, not the transcript. Then add an adversarial framework for security. Two harnesses, disjoint failure sets.

A Python decorator is all you need to trace LLM apps (open-source).

Most LLM evals treat the app like an end-to-end black box.

But LLM apps need component-level evals and tracing since the issue can be anywhere inside the box, like the retriever, tool call, or the LLM itself.

In @deepeval, you can do that with just 3 lines of code:

- Trace individual LLM components (tools, retrievers, generators) with the "@ observe" decorator.
- Attach different metrics to each part.
- Get a visual breakdown of what’s working and what’s not.

Done!

You don't need to refactor any of your existing code.

"Correct Answers from Insufficient Histories: A Controlled Study of Agent Memory Evaluation" — new paper (arXiv preprint, Nov 9, 2026). https://t.co/09pLyRpkI1

In plain terms: agent memory systems hand a model only part of its past history (a trimmed or compressed log), then most evals (automated tests) check the answer against a reference worked out from the FULL history. This paper shows a model can "pass" that check even when the part it was shown could not possibly determine the answer, so a high score can hide lucky guessing.

3 distinct takeaways for product builders:

- A matching answer is not proof the memory worked. With logs cut short so the answer was provably not in view, Qwen3-32B still matched the full-history reference on 87 of 203 cases (DeepSeek-V4-Flash: 85 of 203). Recommendation: in your memory evals, label each test case as "answer is in the context" or "answer is not in the context", and count hits on the second kind as unsupported, not as wins.

- Asking the model to say "I don't know" is not enough. Both prompts explicitly told the model to reply UNDETERMINED when the evidence was missing, yet it gave a concrete answer on 196 of 203 (Qwen) and 182 of 203 (DeepSeek) such cases. Recommendation: if guessing is costly, enforce abstention in code (for example, check whether the retrieved log is complete for the time asked about) instead of relying on the prompt.

- A 99% LLM judge (a model used to grade other models' answers) still slips. The DeepSeek-V4-Flash judge was right on 1,908 of 1,920 constructed cases (99.38%) but twice approved answers the visible log did not support, and two outputs were cut off; a simple rule-based program scored 1,920 of 1,920 with zero model calls. Recommendation: when correctness can be checked by rules, run a deterministic checker first and use the LLM judge only for what rules cannot cover.

Experiment setup (from the paper):
- Environment: synthetic, executable device logs (each report has 8 fields: ids, times, device, action, argument, outcome; duplicates and rejected actions included); 4 query types: count of accepted routes, first route, last route, device state.
- Evidence labels: "insufficient" is proven by building a second legal history that yields byte-identical visible context but a different answer; "sufficient" by public rules (complete-log marker, a complete record after the query cutoff, or first route already visible).
- Readers: hosted Qwen3-32B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, temperature 0, 64-token output limit; 80 confirmation histories, 1,600 requests per reader; context cut to a 768-token budget (a token is roughly a word piece).
- Conditions: raw-text prefix, whole-record prefix, CSV prefix, plus full raw and full CSV controls; the CSV vs raw effect on appropriate answers stayed inconclusive.
- Metrics: reference agreement vs. "context appropriateness" (answer only when the visible log determines it, otherwise abstain); 10,000-replicate bootstrap 95% intervals clustered by history.
- Judge study: 120 held-out histories, 1,920 constructed candidates, compared against finite and extended rule programs and a program-first hybrid.

8 files, 3 roles, 1 repo - turns a product brief into a working app with checks built in.

status lives in the repo, not in your head.

→ CLAUDE.md sets the rules every role has to follow
→ PRODUCT.md holds your brief - the only file you actually write yourself
→ CONTRACT.md turns that brief into a feature contract, line by line
→ FEATURES.json tracks status per feature - built, checked, broken, next
→ HANDOFF.md carries the next action between sessions, so nothing gets re-explained
→ roles/PLANNER.md decides what gets built next
→ roles/BUILDER.md implements it
→ roles/EVALUATOR.md clicks through the actual running app and sends failures straight back to FEATURES.json

run planner, builder and evaluator in the same session and they start agreeing with each other instead of checking each other - keep them separate, that's the rule i broke first and regretted.

AI Architecture: 12 Layers Behind Modern AI Applications (2026)

Building an AI application is much more than connecting an LLM to a chatbot.

A production-ready AI system brings together 12 essential layers:

1. Business Problem – Define what AI needs to solve.
2. Data Layer – Collect data from databases, APIs and documents.
3. Data Processing – Clean, parse, chunk and validate data.
4. Embedding Layer – Convert data into vector representations.
5. Knowledge Layer – Store embeddings in vector databases.
6. Retrieval Layer – Find relevant context using semantic, keyword and hybrid search.
7. Prompt Engineering – Guide model behaviour with prompts and guardrails.
8. AI Model Layer – Use LLMs like GPT, Claude, Gemini and Llama.
9. Agent Layer – Enable planning, reasoning and multi-step execution.
10. Tool Layer – Connect APIs, databases, browsers and external tools.
11. Output Layer – Generate answers, reports, code and workflows.
12. Monitoring & Feedback – Track quality, cost, latency and reliability.

The key takeaway:

An LLM alone doesn't make a production-ready AI application. The real engineering lies in connecting all these layers reliably.

RAG vs. Graph RAG vs. Agentic RAG, clearly explained!

Standard RAG embeds documents into vectors and retrieves the most similar chunks via similarity search. For direct factual lookups, this works well.

But it breaks down when a query needs to connect facts spread across multiple documents. Similarity search retrieves individual chunks, not the relationships between them.

Graph RAG adds a knowledge graph layer on top.

→ During indexing, an LLM extracts entities and relationships from the documents.

→ During retrieval, the system traverses these connections instead of relying on embedding similarity alone.

This is what enables multi-hop queries.

Say a vector DB stores three facts about internal services:

↳ "The checkout service uses payments API."
↳ "The payments API runs on cluster-3."
↳ "Cluster-3 is scheduled for maintenance on Friday."

Someone asks: "Will the checkout service be affected by Friday's maintenance?"

Vector search can likely retrieve facts 1 and 3 because the query mentions "checkout service" and "Friday maintenance."

But it will miss fact 2, which connects the payments API to cluster-3.

That middle fact sits too far from the query in embedding space. It mentions neither "checkout" nor "maintenance," so it never makes it into the retrieved context.

A knowledge graph connects these as linked entities, and graph traversal finds the full path in one query.

Agentic RAG takes a different approach entirely.

Instead of a fixed retrieval pipeline, an LLM agent decides at query time which tools to invoke, which sources to query, and in what order.

Check the visual below to understand the three architectures thoroughly.

One thing to note here is that these three aren't levels of sophistication that you need to graduate through.

Instead, they solve different query types.

↳ Single-hop factual lookups → standard RAG
↳ Multi-hop relationship queries → Graph RAG
↳ Dynamic multi-source tasks with tool use → Agentic RAG

Once the right architecture is in place, the next leverage point is efficiency.

Most RAG architectures rely heavily on vector search, and that layer can be made 32x more memory-efficient using binary quantization.

→ the model only REQUESTS a tool call
→ your app validates, authorizes, and asks a human for risky writes

Try to get an LLM to produce the same outputs twice.  I dare you.

- "seed" is supported in most engines, but not all equally, and it's not enough
- outputs can subtly change sampling when handling 2 simultaneous requests vs. 1
- file system timestamps differing, even unrelated ones, will change the attention heads and desync the output

In Beast, I had to build:
- a FUSE plugin to control all timestamps
- use libfaketime to control what wallclock time various programs get: Node, Python, make, npm, git.  Still some limitations

我在自己的餐厅里装了一个隐藏摄像头。我不在的时候，员工们做的事，改变了一切。

我有过一家餐厅。装了三个 $40 的摄像头（后厨、大堂、门口），围绕它们写了一套软件。OpenCV 配合 YOLOv8 找出画面里的东西。Fable 5 通过 vision API 看画面，判断有没有人需要关心这件事。Telegram 机器人再通知这个人。

工作流程：

> 摄像头把 RTSP 流推到本地服务器
> OpenCV 把视频流切成帧，YOLO 找人、餐具和托盘
> 画面变化超过阈值时，这一帧连同针对该区域写的提示词一起送进 Fable
> Fable 用 JSON 回复，事件类型加优先级
> aiogram 机器人按角色把所有提醒分到不同的聊天里，我的聊天里只有升级上报

它能抓到什么：

> 盘子在保温灯下放了超过 4 分钟。厨师会收到推送，我只有在 6 分钟后仍然没人取走时才会收到
> 客人走后 3 分钟桌子还没收拾（OpenCV 看到的是餐具，没有人）。该区域的服务员会收到桌号，经理在第 5 分钟收到
> 有人走进来，90 秒内没人跟他说话。迎宾员收到推送
> 打烊后每 30 秒拍一张后厨照片，由 Fable 对照打烊清单检查。负责打烊的人会收到那张照片，上面标出了漏掉的地方
> 冰箱门开着 2 分钟以上：先通知副厨，5 分钟后通知我
> 收银台排队 5 人以上，第二个收银台没人，推送给楼面经理
> 后门在打烊后被打开，而当时排班表上没有任何人。我收到一帧画面和时间戳

Fable 的 system prompt 里还有排班表、菜单、打烊清单，以及标了桌号的大堂平面图。提醒长这样："露台 6 号桌，脏餐具已放 7 分钟，最近的空闲服务员是 Marat"。

三个月后：

> 收拾一张桌子的时间从大约 6 分钟降到了不到 3 分钟
> 门口迎接客人的速度快了大约三倍
> 上报给我的事项减少了大约 40%
> 整套东西每月花的钱，比副经理一个班次的工钱还少

头两周员工不太高兴，我能理解。之后他们发现，推送在我发现任何问题之前就到了他们手机上，而我也不再早上 7 点带着火气到店了。洗碗工给自己要了一个专属提醒，大堂快坐满时通知他，好让他提前把干净盘子准备好。

7 月把餐厅卖了。搭系统的时候我算了一笔账：装摄像头之前的那一年，我大约有 10-15% 的营业额，都损失在没人及时看到的事情上。脏桌子，没人的迎宾台。三个 $40 的摄像头一周就解决了这个问题。

之后，经营厨房变得无聊了。我离开了，去做这样的解决方案。

Holy sh*t, researchers just proved that adding a vector database to your AI agent actually degrades its accuracy

every frontier lab is quietly obsessed with harness engineering right now, yet almost nobody explains what it actually does to retrieval

here is the concept explained simply:

think of the model as an analytical engine. brilliant at reasoning, but blind to how much context it consumes

the harness is the loop control, the token budget, and the evidence gate. without it, raw reasoning power drowns in irrelevant text.

naive dense RAG and an agent-native system run the exact same underlying model.
one floods the context window with 512-token chunks and hallucinates on multi-hop questions.
the other surgical-greps pre-compiled claims, hits 91% on FRAMES, and exits in 30 seconds.
the only difference between them is the harness.

in a modern search harness, the architecture is simple:
→ an evidence prefetch that pulls atomic claim-evidence pairs before the first LLM call
→ a strict lexical interface (BM25 + grep) with zero dense vector overhead
→ an evidence gate that verifies sufficiency and halts the loop to prevent token leaks

here is why you need one:
without a harness, you are the control loop.
you manually tune chunk sizes and embedding models.
you watch the agent repeat the same search query three times.
you pay for raw passages the model never uses.
you debug context drift when adjacent chunks contradict each other.

InfiniFlow researchers kept the answering model completely frozen and tested it on complex multi-hop reasoning. with zero vector index and only BM25 and grep, accuracy reached 91% on FRAMES and 85% on BrowseComp-Plus. adding a dense vector leg actually lowered accuracy by introducing competing semantic noise.

three principles of an elite retrieval harness:

1. compile context upstream
extract atomic claim-evidence pairs once at ingestion with verbatim line anchors. stop paying the frontier model to read hundreds of prose pages at runtime.

2. prune the tool surface to lexical anchors
the agent already does the semantic reasoning inside the loop. giving it a dense vector ranking that competes with exact grep anchors only increases hallucination.

3. gate before deep reading
evaluate evidence sufficiency at each step. when the pre-compiled claim suffices, answer immediately. cutting decision latency from 140s to 30s and query tokens by 91%.

how to start:
take the raw documents your agent reads and compile them into verified claim-evidence trees.
take the vector similarity search and replace it with a budgeted BM25 and grep loop backed by an early exit gate.

frontier models are already commoditized.
the harness is where all production value lives.

you’re prompting Claude Fable 5.2 wrong.

these 10 prompting changes could completely change how much you get out of this model, and most people are still using their old Claude workflow.

here’s what you need to change:

1. start at high effort

high gives you the biggest performance improvement per dollar. use extra high when the task demands it. avoid max unless absolutely necessary.

2. make it prove its work

don’t just accept its claims. tell it to run tests, verify the output, and confirm everything works before presenting the result.

3. tell it to finish the job

long agentic tasks can stop prematurely, especially at lower effort levels. give it explicit instructions to complete the entire task.

4. clean up your CLAUDE.md

remove outdated or overly restrictive instructions. too many rules can make the model follow old constraints instead of finding better solutions.

5. understand effort settings

effort controls how much the model thinks. you can’t simply prompt it to skip deliberation like you could with earlier versions.

6. stop asking for internal reasoning

instead of demanding step-by-step internal thought, ask for conclusions, explanations, and evidence behind its decisions.

7. define code ownership

tell it which parts of the codebase it owns. this helps reduce duplicated code and encourages better optimization.

8. remove unnecessary subagent rules

higher effort can trigger its own delegation. forcing subagents everywhere can waste usage.

9. request progress updates

long tasks can run silently for 30–40 minutes. ask Claude to provide brief updates as it works.

10. control response length and tone

effort doesn’t determine how long or detailed the final response should be. specify the format, tone, and level of detail you want.

the biggest lesson?

don’t just give Claude better tasks. give it better instructions for completing them.

A reliable agent needs more than strong reasoning capabilities.

README.md

requirements.txt

Lists the Python packages and dependencies needed by the application.

.env & .gitignore

Protects configuration values while keeping secrets and unnecessary files out.

agent/

Handles planning, state, memory, reasoning loops, and task execution.

tools/

Contains functions for searches, calculations, APIs, databases, and external operations.

models/

Organizes model providers, LLM clients, embeddings, and configuration settings.

prompts/

Keeps system instructions and reusable prompt templates separate from core logic.

utils/

Stores shared helpers, parsers, configuration utilities, and logging functions.

api/

Provides endpoints and schemas for connecting the agent to other applications.

tests/

Checks agent responses, integrations, tools, APIs, and potential failure cases.

data/ & logs/

Holds datasets, reference material, examples, traces, and records for debugging.

AI Architecture: 12 Layers Behind Modern AI Applications (2026)

Building an AI application is much more than connecting an LLM to a chatbot.

A production-ready AI system brings together 12 essential layers:

1. Business Problem – Define what AI needs to solve.
2. Data Layer – Collect data from databases, APIs and documents.
3. Data Processing – Clean, parse, chunk and validate data.
4. Embedding Layer – Convert data into vector representations.
5. Knowledge Layer – Store embeddings in vector databases.

7. Prompt Engineering – Guide model behaviour with prompts and guardrails.
8. AI Model Layer – Use LLMs like GPT, Claude, Gemini and Llama.
9. Agent Layer – Enable planning, reasoning and multi-step execution.
10. Tool Layer – Connect APIs, databases, browsers and external tools.
11. Output Layer – Generate answers, reports, code and workflows.
12. Monitoring & Feedback – Track quality, cost, latency and reliability.

The key takeaway:

An LLM alone doesn't make a production-ready AI application. The real engineering lies in connecting all these layers reliably.

8 AI model architectures, visually explained:

LLMs get so much attention that it's easy to overlook the rest of the field. Different inputs, tasks, and deployment constraints have led to very different model designs.

Here are eight specialized AI model architectures:

1. LLM (Large language models)

Text is split into tokens, mapped to embeddings, and processed through transformer layers. The model generates its response by predicting successive tokens.

↳ GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama.

2. LCM (Large concept models)

Moves prediction to the sentence level. Sentences become SONAR embeddings, and the model predicts the next sentence representation. Meta explored both autoregressive and diffusion-based versions.

↳ Meta's LCM research introduced this approach.

3. LAM (Large action models)

Connects a user's request to actions in an environment. These systems interpret intent, plan steps, and use interfaces or tools, often checking results before continuing.

↳ Rabbit R1, Microsoft UFO, Claude Computer Use.

4. MoE (Mixture of experts)

A router assigns token representations to selected expert networks inside the model. Activating a subset of experts adds model capacity without running every expert for every token.

↳ Mixtral, DeepSeek, Switch Transformer.

5. VLM (Vision-language models)

Combines visual representations with language processing. A vision encoder extracts image features, which are connected to a language model so it can answer questions about visual content.

↳ GPT-4V, Gemini, LLaVA.

6. SLM (Small language models)

Uses fewer parameters to reduce memory and compute requirements. These models can run locally, with quantization often reducing their deployment footprint further.

↳ Phi-3, Gemma, Mistral 7B, Llama 3.2 1B.

7. MLM (Masked language models)

Learns by predicting hidden tokens using context on both sides. This bidirectional training produces representations useful for retrieval, classification, and other language-understanding tasks.

↳ BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa.

8. SAM (Segment Anything Model)

An image encoder processes the image, while a prompt encoder handles points, boxes, or masks. A mask decoder combines them to identify the requested regions.

↳ Meta's SAM supports interactive segmentation and image annotation.

These aren't eight mutually exclusive categories. A small model can process images, and a language model can use MoE layers. Some labels describe architecture, while others describe training or intended use.

There's another approach I kept outside the image because it alters how a model handles context rather than introducing a separate model family.

Recursive language models, from MIT, put the input into a Python environment that a root model can inspect through code.

The model can search or slice that input, then make recursive model calls on selected portions instead of loading everything into its own context window.

The reported experiments handled inputs beyond 10 million tokens without retraining, with gains over the base model even on some tasks whose inputs already fit its context window.

I recently wrote a full breakdown of how this works, including why accessing a large input and reasoning reliably over it are different problems.

Read it below.

Anthropic released two models this week and published a number about them that matters more than any benchmark on the page.

In as many as 43% of automated audit transcripts, Claude Mythos 5.2 appeared to recognise it might be under evaluation.

That figure is Anthropic's own, from their system card.

Why it matters is a measurement problem before it's anything else. 

Every behavioural evaluation rests on an assumption borrowed from experimental design: that the subject behaves the same whether or not it knows it's being watched. 

In human research that assumption fails often enough to have a name & the standard remedies like blinding & deception work precisely because the subject can't tell the difference.

When the subject can tell the difference, the evaluation stops measuring behaviour & starts measuring behaviour-under-observation. Those are the same quantity only if the subject doesn't distinguish them.

Anthropic also reports that Mythos 5.2 is the 1st model they've tested that got past a reasoning monitor while instructed to underperform, succeeding roughly one attempt in four. 

A reasoning monitor reads a model's intermediate steps looking for signs it's deliberately doing badly. Getting past one means generating a chain of reasoning that reads as genuine effort while the answer is deliberately worse. 

They say this makes real-world behaviour harder to judge & that they expect the problem to grow.

Set against that, the same system card reports a real improvement on a different axis. In tests with a deliberately weakened sandbox, Mythos 5.2 reached for credentials or files outside its boundary in 3.1 percent of scenarios. Mythos 5.1 did it 21% of the time. Mythos 5 did it 39%.

One measure improved by an order of magnitude while confidence in any measure got worse. Not contradictory findings, these are  findings about different things.

The rest, briefly. Fable 5.2 & Mythos 5.2 are the same underlying model, differing only in safeguards: Fable carries cyber and biology classifiers and is open to everyone, Mythos runs without them for organisations vetted through Anthropic's verification programmes. Eight dollars per million input tokens, forty output, down 20 percent from 5.1. A million-token context window, 128K output cap, June 2026 cutoff. The benchmark figures come from Anthropic's launch page and have not been independently reproduced.

The benchmarks will be reproduced or they won't. The evaluation-awareness number is the one worth watching, because it governs how much any of the others mean.

🤖 Day 10/30 - AI Agents Series

In the last post, we learned how Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) allows AI agents to retrieve relevant information from external knowledge before generating responses. Today, we'll explore the technology that makes semantic search possible—embeddings and vector databases.

Embeddings and Vector Databases – FAISS, ChromaDB, and Pinecone

Traditional databases search using exact keywords. AI agents, however, need to understand the meaning behind text, even when different words are used. This is made possible through embeddings and vector databases.

What Are Embeddings?

Embeddings are numerical vector representations of text generated by AI models.

Instead of storing words as plain text, embeddings capture their semantic meaning.

For example, the sentences:

→ "How do I deploy a Docker container?"

→ "How can I run my application using Docker?"

have different wording but similar meanings, so their embeddings will be close together in vector space.

This allows AI systems to perform semantic search rather than simple keyword matching.

What Is a Vector Database?

A vector database stores embeddings and retrieves the most semantically similar vectors for a given query.

When a user asks a question, the workflow is:

→ Convert the question into an embedding

→ Search the vector database

→ Retrieve the most similar document chunks

→ Pass the retrieved context to the LLM

→ Generate an informed response

This retrieval process is the foundation of modern RAG applications.

FAISS

FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) is an open-source library developed by Meta for efficient similarity search.

Features include:

→ Extremely fast vector search

→ Optimized for large datasets

→ Runs locally

→ Supports millions of embeddings

FAISS is ideal for high-performance local AI applications.

ChromaDB

ChromaDB is an open-source vector database designed specifically for AI applications.

Benefits include:

→ Simple Python integration

→ Persistent storage

→ Metadata filtering

→ Ideal for RAG prototypes

It is one of the easiest vector databases to use when building AI agents.

Pinecone

Pinecone is a fully managed cloud vector database.

It provides:

→ Automatic indexing

→ High availability

→ Horizontal scalability

→ Low-latency semantic search

→ Managed infrastructure

Pinecone is well suited for production AI systems that require scalable vector search without managing servers.

Choosing the Right Vector Database

→ FAISS for fast local similarity search

→ ChromaDB for lightweight RAG applications and development

→ Pinecone for cloud-native, production-scale deployments

The choice depends on your application's scale, infrastructure, and deployment requirements.

Project: Create a Searchable Knowledge Base

Today we'll build a searchable knowledge base powered by embeddings and a vector database.

Our application will:

→ Load documents from a local folder

→ Split documents into smaller chunks

→ Generate embeddings for each chunk

→ Store embeddings in a vector database

→ Accept natural language questions

→ Perform semantic similarity search

→ Retrieve the most relevant information

→ Return accurate, context-aware answers using an LLM

By the end of this project, you'll have a reusable knowledge base that can search documents based on meaning rather than exact keywords—the foundation for intelligent document search, enterprise AI assistants, and advanced RAG systems.

Most People Get This Wrong: Vector Search

Most people pick the wrong one. What's yours?

Your question gets turned into a vector by an embedding model, and that vector is what the database searches.

Did you get it right?

What happens when you combine embedding models with System 1 decision models? You get the intersection, which is VENN —> Vector Decision Models, a very cool OSS research project from Mark Russinovich that I was fortunate to review early and am excited to support.

An agent's memory can be a file you back up and move between machines, rather than another database service you have to keep running. 💾

Memvid packages content, metadata and search structures into a portable .mv2 file, with a Rust core and interfaces for other application stacks.

The project describes its storage as an append-only sequence of immutable “Smart Frames,” each carrying content information, timestamps and checksums. The current design borrows an organizational idea from video encoding; it is not a requirement to turn your documents into a playable video.

🧩 The basic developer workflow is tangible:

▪️ Create a memory file.
▪️ Add documents with titles, source URIs and tags.
▪️ Commit the changes.
▪️ Search and retrieve matching content.
▪️ Inspect entries through timeline-oriented queries.

The repository includes an example that performs those steps and reports whether the file has lexical, vector and time indexes.

That is useful for a project assistant whose knowledge needs to travel with the project. The data and retrieval structure can be treated as an artifact rather than reconstructed from a running service every time.

🔎 Search capabilities depend on the features you enable. The documented Rust options include BM25 full-text search, vector similarity with local embeddings and optional cloud API embeddings. Other feature flags add document or media processing.

Those are building blocks, rather than an automatic guarantee that every stored fact will be recalled correctly. The application still decides what to ingest, what to ask for and how retrieved material enters the model's context.

The current core is Apache-2.0, with a Rust 1.85+ requirement. The project also links a CLI, Node.js SDK and Python SDK, plus a public online sandbox.

📌 Local retrieval can be used without a hosted database. Selecting a cloud embedding provider or using an online demo introduces its own network processing, so those paths should not be confused with an entirely offline setup.

For an initial test, I would use a small collection with known answers and inspect the retrieved sources. Portability is attractive; useful recall still has to be demonstrated on your actual material.

#AIAgents #RAG #LocalAI #OpenSource

🔎 Search text, images and video frames with one encoder, then use the same model to choose between predefined answers.

MetaEncoder v1 from Meta combines multimodal retrieval and closed-set decisions in a roughly 28.4B-parameter model using the Muse Glimmer architecture.

Its interface has three main operations:

▪️ encode: turn content into an embedding for storage, clustering or comparison.
▪️ retrieve: rank a collection against a query.
▪️ decide: answer predefined questions about a state, with scores and probabilities.

🧩 Each embedding is a normalized 6,656-dimensional vector. An input can contain text, images, video frames or a mixture of them.

Instructions tell the model what the representation is for. A document and a search query can use different instructions, and the same image can produce different embeddings depending on the task.

For video, the wrapper accepts a list of frames. If you supply more than eight, it uniformly subsamples them to eight.

You can also encode a corpus once and reuse its vectors for repeated searches. The wrapper returns float32 embeddings and cosine-similarity rankings; it does not build a compressed vector database for you.

⚖️ The interesting part is decide. Give it a scenario and questions such as “Is this a shopping request?” or “Which category fits this image?” It embeds the question and candidate answers, compares their similarity, and selects an option.

Supported outputs include yes/no, a choice among 2–26 options, and a score over ordered labels.

Probabilities come from a softmax over similarity scores, using the contrastive training temperature of 0.02. The included calibration method can fit that temperature to labeled examples from your own task. A sharply peaked distribution describes the model’s preference among those options, rather than proving the answer correct.

🛠️ The release includes downloadable weights and a Python wrapper. It requires transformers 5.15 or newer, and the model card says one 80 GB GPU holds the model in bf16.

For document search, media tagging and routing, the practical appeal is reusing one representation model across retrieval and structured decisions. There is no generated explanation to parse: the output is the selected value and its associated scores.

• Combine retrieved chunks

• Send prompt + context to the LLM
