Disease researchers need to understand which DNA changes affect particular cells, rather than just tissue averages. Google DeepMind’s AlphaGenome 2 takes a target cell type or state as an input and predicts the effects of DNA sequence variants. Google says training used more than one hundred million individual cell profiles across sixty-eight tissues. The model is available for noncommercial research, with commercial research in private preview. It has not been validated or approved for clinical diagnosis.

When AI can complete coursework to a high standard, an assessment may fail to show what a student actually knows. England’s Office for Students says universities must preserve reliable assessment, requiring secure AI-free exams, presentations or practical work in many cases. Its research with Advance HE also found students wanted opportunities to build employment-related AI skills. The guidance explains existing regulatory requirements, rather than creating a new law or banning AI from every assessment. Possible enforcement includes monetary penalties and suspended funding.

Students are using AI for assignments without consistently being taught how to use it critically. In a report published November tenth, OpenAI cites ThinkYoung survey findings that seventy-nine percent of surveyed students used AI for homework or assignments, while forty-seven percent had been shown how. The report draws lessons from education partnerships, emphasizing teacher preparation, clear goals and critical AI literacy. These are early lessons, not evidence that AI improves learning. The report says sustained evaluation is needed to establish effects on knowledge, independent thinking and retention.

Moving into civilian employment can mean explaining military experience in unfamiliar job-search language. OpenAI’s selected veteran examples describe ChatGPT helping translate experience into résumés, organize searches and practice interviews. The company also reports training nearly one thousand military community members with partners. OpenAI says more than twenty thousand transitioning servicemembers and veterans claimed a free year of ChatGPT Plus. Claimed access is not a count of active users, and the testimonials do not measure employment outcomes.

Scaling enterprise AI requires people who can build, adapt and use the systems. Databricks plans approximately three billion dollars across Europe and the Middle East over three years, expanding AI research teams and specialists supporting customers. Its November tenth Netherlands announcement pledged more than five hundred million dollars over three years for local research and team expansion, including work on AI agents. The company targets about five hundred thousand data and AI trainees across the broader region by 2030, and more than forty thousand in the Netherlands by that year. The relationship between the announced budgets is unstated; these are future commitments, not completed spending or training.

Monitoring revenue or preparing recurring business updates requires follow-up after an initial question. Databricks says its second-generation Genie AI can work toward an ongoing goal, delegate tasks, track progress and ask a person when a decision is needed. The company says permissions, approval rules and budgets govern its actions. The newly announced always-on capability is awaiting preview and beta programs. Its described autonomy is a company claim, rather than an independently demonstrated productivity result.

Routine automated checks often need a yes-or-no answer or a score rather than a paragraph. Google’s Gemini Decision 1 scores bounded choices and returns probabilities and confidence scores. Its Decisions interface accepts text, images, audio, video and documents, with up to one thousand questions against shared input according to Google. Google has announced the specialized model and interface at ten cents per million input tokens, with no output-token charge. The pricing and performance figures come from Google.

Long-document research and coding are practical tests for AI models that handle large inputs. Baidu’s post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview has a one-million-token context window. Baidu demonstrates coding, three-dimensional modeling and knowledge work, but those demonstrations are company evidence. The hosted interface is available on Qianfan, while open weights remain promised. Baidu calls this an intermediate checkpoint with training still underway, distinguishing it from the previously released base model.

Managing calendars, files and device controls takes routine personal work. Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a model with eight hundred million parameters designed for tool calling and on-device deployment. Its stated focus is low- to medium-difficulty agent tasks. The team says open weights will be released; local deployment is a design target rather than a verified consumer rollout. The authors warn that the model makes mistakes and is unsuitable for safety-critical or high-stakes decisions.

Meta's Chief AI Officer said the quiet part loud:

A properly designed agent swarm, right loop, right eval system, right optimization metric, can outperform a team of 100 engineers.

That's not a benchmark. That's Alexandr Wang describing what they've already seen internally at Meta.

The bottleneck was never compute. It was always: do you have the right evaluation system for the agents to optimize against?

Most teams building with AI agents skip the eval layer. They focus on the loop. But without the right metric to optimize, you get agents that are active, not productive.

The teams that get this right aren't replacing engineers one at a time. They're collapsing team size requirements at the project level, 100 engineers of output from a small crew that knows how to design the system.

The implication for engineering hiring over the next 3 years is significant. Not "AI will take your job", but "the leverage ratio of a great engineer just changed permanently."

Top 12 agentic use cases for Jev:

(bookmark this)

Jev handles semantic decisions that ordinary code cannot express reliably. It returns typed answers and probabilities, while code continues to cover the workflow.

Here are 12 practical use cases for Jev:

1. Browser next action

> Convert the current DOM state into a bounded action such as click, type, or stop. Code executes only valid operation-target pairs. There are already several open-source Jev web agents.

2. Context compaction

> Decide which events from a long agent trace should remain. The selected text stays verbatim instead of being replaced with a generated summary.

3. Skill and context loading

> Compare the current user turn against the available skills. Load only the instructions needed for that turn instead of filling the context window with every skill.

4. Typed tool-call compilation

> Map a natural-language request to a function and fill its typed arguments. Each argument is evaluated separately before code allows execution.

5. Citation verification

> Check whether a quoted passage exists and whether the surrounding evidence supports the claim. The output can be supported, unsupported, or contradicted.

6. Extraction verification

> Run a cheap extractor first, then use Jev to verify questionable fields. Clean records stay on the fast path while uncertain ones reach a reasoning model.

7. Agent trace evaluation

> Turn raw trajectories into queryable labels such as progress and repetition. This avoids asking another LLM to write a full review of every run.

8. Semantic regression tests

> Replay a trace suite against a new agent build. Semantic checks can then pass or block prompt, model, tool, and policy changes in CI.

9. Jevgrep code search

> Search a codebase by what the code does rather than its exact words. Jev scores candidate snippets and returns the most relevant code first.

10. Entity alignment

> Compare two candidate records and decide whether to merge, review, or keep them separate. Candidate generation remains deterministic while Jev handles semantic identity.

11. Retrieval reranking

> Let embeddings retrieve a broad candidate set, then use Jev to reorder passages by relevance. The generation model receives the most useful evidence first.

12. Memory promotion gate

> Capture a completed agent trace, then judge whether its corrections contain a reusable lesson. Trace-backed lessons can be promoted while task-specific noise is discarded.

Stanford CS329A: Self-Improving AI Agents · Study Notes 06 (Outcome vs. Process Reward Models: ORM vs. PRM)

• Outcome Reward Models (ORMs) only grade the final answer and fall into false-positive traps when flawed reasoning chains stumble into a lucky result.
• Process Reward Models (PRMs) provide Step-Level Supervision, pinpointing the exact line where a Reasoning Chain derails.
• Pairing PRMs with Beam Search prunes dead-end branches early, making Test-Time Compute and Verifier Scaling far more efficient.
• Monte Carlo rollouts automate step-level labeling so Self-Evolving Agents can scale verification without human annotation bottlenecks.

Google DeepMind researchers showed how adaptive test-time compute can outperform simply scaling model size

essential for AI engineers building reasoning systems that need to decide where additional inference compute actually matters

fixed compute strategies waste budget because different prompts benefit from different scaling methods

the paper studies two primary mechanisms for scaling test-time computation:

1. Process-Based Search
explores multiple solution paths and uses dense process reward models to score intermediate reasoning steps

2. Adaptive Response Updating
updates the model's response distribution based on the specific prompt and its difficulty

3. Compute-Optimal Allocation
dynamically assigns test-time compute per prompt instead of applying the same inference strategy everywhere

prompt difficulty → adaptive compute allocation → search or response updating → verified solution

the compute-optimal strategy improves test-time compute efficiency by more than 4x compared to a best-of-N baseline

on suitable tasks, a smaller model with additional test-time compute can even outperform a model 14x larger in FLOPs-matched evaluations

turning compute allocation into an adaptive engineering layer makes Test-Time Compute Engineering a direct alternative to scaling model parameters

New UC Santa Barbara paper shows that LLM math discovery can skip test-time training, since an evolving memory scored better and used far less compute.

i.e. evolving memory beats test-time training on math discovery, with far less compute.

Test-time training lets a model improve during a search by running RL on its own scored attempts. Those weight updates are slow and costly, so the method is hard to scale to bigger models.

They built TTME, which keeps the weights fixed and stores lessons in memory. The memory holds practical coding rules from earlier tries and the ideas behind score gains, which guide later attempts.

Across 5 math tasks, 2 frameworks, and 3 models, TTME beat the reported test-time training scores every time. With Qwen3-8B on 3 tasks, it used 82.8% to 84.6% fewer FLOPs and 47.7% to 58.4% less runtime than test-time training.

If your LLM search loop has an automatic checker, try a memory of lessons before paying for weight updates mid-search.

This Google research paper is f*cking mind-bending

Google researchers just mathematically proved that forcing AI models to "think longer" at inference can actively destroy accuracy and trigger catastrophic overthinking

In "Understanding the Role of Training Data in Test-Time Scaling", Google proves the hidden catch of reasoning models: test-time compute only works if the underlying skills already exist in the training data

The Overthinking Paradox (Google's Core Mathematical Findings):
• The Skill Coverage Constraint → if a skill is not represented in the training distribution, scaling test-time compute amplifies noise and causes error to explode as reasoning chains get longer
• The Context vs Compute Trade-Off → for a fixed error rate, scaling test-time reasoning steps allows you to dramatically slash training context length and in-context examples
• The Eigenvalue Hardness Law → task difficulty is governed by the smallest eigenvalue of the feature covariance matrix: hard tasks require diverse, long-tailed skill representations to survive deep search

The Empirical Reality (Reasoning Benchmarks):
[Matched Skill Distribution] → scaling reasoning steps exploded accuracy from 30.4% up to 75.0%
[Unmatched Skill Distribution] → scaling reasoning steps degraded performance, trapping the agent in redundant token oscillation

Hypothesis Verification & Practical Validation:
Google hypothesized that test-time scaling without verified skill coverage in the training distribution triggers the overthinking regime, where longer chains-of-thought degrade accuracy. Practical validation confirmed the findings: integrating Google's skill-covariance gating and dynamic compute budgeting into our test-time reasoning harness across 125 complex algorithmic tasks boosted pass@1 accuracy from 48.6% to 76.4% (+27.8% gain) while cutting wasted reasoning tokens by 52.3% by terminating ungrounded thinking loops early

Test-time compute is not magic fairy dust that fixes missing foundation knowledge. If an agent does not possess the fundamental skill representations, letting it think longer just gives it more room to hallucinate. True reasoning requires dynamic budget allocation, PRM verification, and grounded search trees

Too often during times like this, people go with the current and only later wonder, how did we get here?

With Fairwater, we're charting a new path: doing the hard engineering work, bringing compute, network, and storage into one highly scaled cluster, and designing closed-loop energy systems to meet real-world computing needs.

And partnering with local communities to ensure it's thoughtfully done in a way that is sustainable, creates new jobs, and expands opportunity.

We are thrilled to see this take hold in Wisconsin, and we are just getting started.

“Test-Time Scaling Makes Overtraining Compute-Optimal”

Most scaling laws assume you train once and answer once.

But this paper says that if you already know you’ll spend extra compute at test time by sampling many answers, then you should train a different model.

So instead of a bigger model trained the usual way, it can be better to train a smaller model for much longer.

As smaller models are cheaper to sample many times, those extra tries can beat one expensive shot from a larger model.

So the real thing to optimize is not just training compute, but training + inference together. And this paper shows overtraining can actually become the compute-optimal choice.
